589.title: Known in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13–35)
589.hook: two disciples, seven miles, burning hearts, and bread broken at dusk
589.howItsDone: Some churches describe their Sunday worship in the shape of the Emmaus story: first the scriptures read and explained, then bread broken at the Lord's table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leros, idle tales, and women who were right first. Your line: he is not here.

The same Sunday, late afternoon. Two of Jesus's followers are walking out of Jerusalem toward a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. One is named Cleopas; the other Luke never names. They're going over it and over it, the way people do after a funeral. A stranger catches up and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know what happened? And they tell him, ending in the past tense, in the King James words: "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel."

We trusted. Past. Their hope is something that used to be. They even mention the women's report about the empty tomb, and it hasn't helped. Luke tells us their eyes were holden, kept from recognizing him. Then the stranger begins with Moses and all the prophets and walks them through everything in the scriptures about himself, seven miles of it. At the village it's getting dark, and he acts as if he's going on. They press him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." That plea later gave a hymn its title, Abide with Me. So he stays. At the table, the guest does the host's job: he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them, the same four movements as the feeding of the five thousand, and the last supper. "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight." And then, looking at each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?" They go back to Jerusalem that same hour, and tell how he was known of them in breaking of bread. Some Christians hear this story as the shape of their Sunday worship: the scriptures opened, then the bread broken. He wasn't recognized in the explaining. He was recognized at the table.
screen: `WE TRUSTED: HOPE IN THE PAST TENSE.`
then, large: `KNOWN OF THEM IN BREAKING OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who's been walking with you lately, maybe without you really noticing: a neighbor, a new coworker, a friend who's been quiet. Picture the moment they'd usually head home, and you saying, stay, it's getting late, eat with us, and breaking ordinary bread together. If you pray, you can ask to recognize God in the people at your table.
Cleopas. One of the two disciples walking to Emmaus who didn't recognize the risen Jesus until he broke the bread at their table.
Your line: abide with us. The day was far spent, and he stayed. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

590.title: A piece of broiled fish (Luke 24:36–49)
590.hook: he's no ghost: touch me, see my hands, give me something to eat
590.howItsDone: Christians confess in the ancient creeds belief in the resurrection of the body, and many churches read this appearance in the weeks after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cleopas at Emmaus, and Jesus known in the breaking of bread. Your line: abide with us.

The two from Emmaus have just burst back into the room in Jerusalem. The others tell them, the Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon. And the two tell their story of the road and the bread. While they're still talking, Jesus himself is standing in the middle of them. He says, in the King James words, "Peace be unto you." And everyone in the room, people who just said they believed, is terrified. Luke says they thought they were seeing a spirit. A ghost. Which is exactly what anyone would think.

Jesus asks why they're troubled, and then he does something very physical. "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have." Handle me. Touch me. Then a line that sounds like a real room full of people: "And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered." They can't believe it, not from doubt, but because it's too good. And Jesus answers with the most ordinary question in the world: "Have ye here any meat?" Meat meant food of any kind. They give him a piece of broiled fish, and he takes it and eats it in front of them. Christian writers from the second century on made a lot of this small scene. The risen Jesus isn't a vision or a memory or an idea. He has hands with wounds in them. He eats what's on the table. Christians teach that the resurrection is of the body, and Luke wants you to see a body. Then he opens their understanding of the scriptures and gives them a job: to preach repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things, he says. But first, wait in the city until you're clothed with power from on high. That next chapter is Luke's second book, Acts. Today's is smaller: a frightened room, wounded hands, and a piece of fish.
screen: then, large: `A SPIRIT HATH NOT FLESH AND BONES.`

segments.voice: If you have something small to eat nearby, a piece of fruit, a cracker, look at it first, its color and weight, then eat it slowly, the way you'd eat in front of someone you hadn't seen in a long time. Let yourself be glad, simply, that you have a body, and food, and this minute; if there's no food near you, just notice your hands and feet. If you pray, you can give thanks before you eat.
Resurrection. What the risen Jesus proved to his frightened friends by showing his wounded hands and eating a piece of broiled fish in front of them.
Your line: handle me and see. Not a ghost: hands, feet, and a meal. See you tomorrow.

591.title: Luke close: great joy (Luke 24:50–53)
591.hook: he blesses them with lifted hands; they return with great joy and are always in the temple
591.tomorrow: in the beginning was the Word
591.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter, and in some churches services end the way Luke's Gospel does, with a minister lifting hands to bless the people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, resurrection: wounded hands, a piece of broiled fish, and friends too joyful to believe. Your line: handle me and see.

Ninety days ago, Luke's Gospel opened in the temple in Jerusalem. An old priest named Zechariah was burning incense, and an angel told him he'd have a son. He didn't believe it, and he came out of the sanctuary unable to speak. The people outside were waiting for him, and he could only make signs with his hands. Today, on the last page, Luke finishes the sentence he started on the first.

Luke's last four verses, in the King James words: "And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven. And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: And were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God." Lifted hands. In Leviticus, Aaron the priest lifts up his hands toward the people and blesses them. Some readers see Luke closing a circle: a Gospel that opened with a priest who came out speechless ends with Jesus blessing his friends with his hands raised, still blessing as he's taken up. Then the joy. Not long before, these same people were frightened, grieving, calling the women's news idle tales. Now he's gone from their sight, and they go back with great joy, in the temple every day, praising God. Luke started in the temple, and he ends there. Look back over these ninety days. Zechariah and Elizabeth. Mary's song. Shepherds on the night shift. Simeon holding the child. The sermon at Nazareth. The good Samaritan. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son. Zacchaeus in the tree. The widow's two coins. The upper room, the garden, the look across the courtyard, a criminal promised paradise, bread broken at Emmaus. Luke said at the start he was writing so his reader would know these things were certain. He ends not with an argument, but with joy, and blessing, and people praising God.
screen: `HE LIFTED UP HIS HANDS, AND BLESSED.`
then, large: `RETURNED TO JERUSALEM WITH GREAT JOY.`

segments.voice: If you can, lift your hands a little, palms out or up, and bring the people in your life to mind one at a time: someone at home, someone at work, someone far away, someone you're struggling with. As each one comes, wish them good: peace, rest, joy. If you pray, you can use the old blessing from the book of Numbers, The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; if you don't, simply hold them in good will.
Luke close. The end of Luke's Gospel: Jesus blessing his friends with lifted hands, and the friends going home with great joy, praising God in the temple.
Your line: with great joy. Tomorrow, a new Gospel: John, starting before the beginning. Ninety days of Luke, done.

592.title: In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1–5)
592.hook: John starts before Genesis: the Word was with God and was God
592.carry: the light shines in the darkness
592.howItsDone: Some churches read the opening of John's Gospel on Christmas Day, and in the older form of the Latin Mass it was read at the end as the 'Last Gospel'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of Luke: lifted hands, a blessing, and great joy. Your line: with great joy.

Matthew starts with a family tree. Mark starts with John the Baptist in the desert. Luke starts with an old priest in the temple. John starts before any of them: before Bethlehem, before Abraham, before the world. His first words are the first words of the Bible. In the beginning. Anyone who knew Genesis would hear it at once: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And in Genesis, God creates by speaking. God said, let there be light, and there was light. For the next sixty-five days, John's Gospel, in order. Today, its first five verses, and its first great word.

Here it is, in the King James words: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made." The Word, in Greek, is Logos. It means word, but much more: a spoken message, an account, a reason, the sense that makes something make sense. The word logic comes from it, and the ending of words like biology. Some Greek philosophers had used logos for the reason running through the universe. Jewish readers knew God's word that creates, and Wisdom, who in Proverbs is there with God at creation. John picks up a word both worlds would hear, and goes further than either: the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Christians read this as a statement about Jesus: God's own Word, there before creation, the one through whom everything was made. Then light. "In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." That last Greek verb can carry two meanings. It can mean grasp, understand: the darkness didn't comprehend the light. It can also mean seize, overpower: the darkness didn't put it out. Translators pick one; John may mean both. Either way, notice the tense. The light shineth. Present tense. Still shining, while you listen.
screen: `THE WORD WAS WITH GOD, AND WAS GOD.`
then, large: `THE LIGHT SHINETH IN DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Say the first verse slowly, now or later from a Bible: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Then sit with the last line, the light shineth in darkness, and picture one small light in a dark room: a candle, a phone screen, a streetlight through a window. The dark around it is large, and the light is still there.
Logos. Greek for word, reason and meaning. John's name for the one who was in the beginning with God, and was God.
Your line: the light shines in the darkness. Sixty-five days of John begin here. Day five hundred ninety-two, done.

593.title: Full of grace and truth (John 1:6–18)
593.hook: the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us
593.howItsDone: In the Angelus, a traditional Catholic prayer, people bow or kneel at the line 'and the Word was made flesh', and some churches bow in the Creed at the words about the incarnation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Logos: the Word in the beginning, and a light the darkness can't put out. Your line: the light shines in the darkness.

A tent goes up in a field, right next to yours. Same mud, same rain, same mosquitoes. Somebody has decided to camp where you camp. In the book of Exodus, the people of Israel live in tents in the wilderness, and in the middle of the camp stands a tent for God: the tabernacle, which the glory of the LORD fills. John has said the Word was with God in the beginning. Today he says how the Word came close, and he says it with a tent.

First, a man sent from God named John, the Baptist, who came as a witness to the light. He wasn't the light, John says carefully; he came to point to it. Then the light comes into the world, and the world doesn't know him. He came to his own, and his own didn't receive him. But to as many as did, he gave power to become children of God. Then, in the King James words: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth." Made flesh. Not a costume, not a visit: skin, hunger, tiredness. Christians call this the incarnation, from the Latin for in flesh. And dwelt: the Greek verb literally means pitched a tent. The Word set up camp among us, the way God's presence lived in the tabernacle. Full of grace and truth. Grace is a gift you didn't earn; truth is what's real, even when it's hard. It's easy to find one without the other: kindness that won't be honest, or honesty that isn't kind. John says in this one person they come together. Then: "And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace." The Greek is grace instead of grace, or grace on top of grace, and some modern versions say grace upon grace, like waves arriving on a shore. And the passage ends: no one has ever seen God, but the one close to the Father's heart has made him known.
screen: then, large: `OF HIS FULNESS HAVE ALL WE RECEIVED.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who told you something true and hard, and stayed kind while saying it, a coach, a parent, a friend, a doctor: it stung, and you knew they were on your side. Then picture someone who needs a true word from you, and imagine saying it gently, with no wish to win. If you pray, ask for both.
Skene, the Greek word for a tent, the root of dwelt, pitched his tent: how John describes the Word made flesh, camping among us full of grace and truth.
Your line: grace upon grace. One gift arriving on top of another. See you tomorrow.

594.title: The Lamb of God (John 1:19–34)
594.hook: John the Baptist points away from himself: behold the Lamb
594.howItsDone: In the Catholic Mass, and in Lutheran and Anglican communion services that keep it, the congregation sings or says the Agnus Dei, a short chant built on John the Baptist's words, Lamb of God, before receiving the bread and wine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, skene: the Word made flesh, pitching a tent among us, full of grace and truth. Your line: grace upon grace.

A delegation has walked out from Jerusalem to the river, priests and Levites, with one job: find out who this man is. People are talking about John the Baptist, and every question they bring is a chance for him to make himself bigger. Who are you? Are you the Christ? No. Are you Elijah? No. Are you that prophet? No. Then who? Give us an answer for the people who sent us. What do you say about yourself?
screen: `NOT THE CHRIST, NOT ELIJAH, NOT THE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: His answer, in the King James words: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Esaias." Not a name. A voice: something that exists to carry a message, then fades. About the one coming after him, he says he isn't worthy to undo his sandal strap, a servant's job. The next day, he sees Jesus walking toward him, and he points: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." Readers have heard more than one lamb in that title. The Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt on the night of freedom. The lambs offered morning and evening at the altar, in the book of Exodus. And the servant in Isaiah, brought as a lamb to the slaughter. Readers differ on which one John the Baptist meant; the Gospel may want all of them. Later in this Gospel, Jesus is condemned on the day John calls the preparation of the Passover. Then John tells what he saw at the river: the Spirit coming down from heaven like a dove, and staying on him. He didn't know who it would be until he saw that. I saw, he says, and I bear witness that this is the Son of God. Notice what John the Baptist does with all his fame. He uses it to point. Behold. That's the one. And the very next day, two of his own disciples will follow his finger and leave him.
screen: then, large: `BEHOLD THE LAMB OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose good work goes unnoticed: a teammate who fixed the problem you got credit for, a quietly kind friend, a nurse, a neighbor. Picture pointing to them out loud, the way John pointed, behold, look at what this person did; it doesn't make you smaller, it makes you a voice. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.
Amnos, the Greek word for a young sheep, a lamb: John the Baptist's name for Jesus as he pointed him out, the one who takes away the sin of the world.
Your line: behold the lamb. A voice, not a name, pointing away from itself. That's five hundred ninety-four.

595.title: Come and see (John 1:35–42)
595.hook: two disciples follow; he asks, what are you looking for?
595.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate Andrew, the first called, on November 30, and Christians often describe sharing their faith the way he did, by bringing a friend or family member to come and see.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amnos, the Lamb of God, and a man who spent his fame pointing away from himself. Your line: behold the lamb.

The next day, John the Baptist is standing with two of his own disciples when Jesus walks past. John says it again: behold the Lamb of God. And the two start walking after Jesus. Think about what that cost John: his students, leaving. And think what it's like for the two of them, following a stranger at a distance, not sure what they'll say if he notices. Then he does. He turns around and sees them following. And the first words Jesus speaks in John's whole Gospel are a question.

The question, in the King James words: "What seek ye?" What are you looking for? Not who are you, not what do you want from me. It's a question for anyone, any day. They answer with a question of their own: "Rabbi, (which is to say, being interpreted, Master,) where dwellest thou?" Where are you staying? They don't want a quick answer in the road; they want to be where he is. And he says: "Come and see." No speech. No test. An invitation. Then John adds a detail only an eyewitness would bother with, many readers think: "for it was about the tenth hour." Around four in the afternoon. Someone remembered the time of day for the rest of their life. One of the two is named: Andrew. The other is never named, and many Christians through the centuries have thought it was the beloved disciple, though the text doesn't say. The first thing Andrew does is find his own brother, Simon, and tell him: "We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ." He brings him to Jesus, and Jesus gives Simon a new name: Cephas, Aramaic for rock. In Greek, Petros. Peter. Look at the chain: John points, two follow, a question, an invitation, an afternoon, and one of them goes to get his brother. That's how this Gospel says it began: not with a crowd, but with someone saying, come and see.

Let Jesus's first question in John sit in front of you: what are you looking for? Not what you should want, but what you actually want underneath, peace, to be known, a second chance, rest, and let one honest answer come without fixing or judging it. If you pray, you can tell God your answer.
Cephas. The Aramaic name, meaning rock, that Jesus gives Simon when Andrew brings his brother to him, Peter in Greek.
Your line: what seek ye? A week from Emmaus to the end of Luke, then into John: the Word, the Lamb, and this first invitation. Day five hundred ninety-five, and another week on the path.
